steps.title: Same three letters, related meanings
body: Most Arabic words are built from a root — usually three consonants carrying a core meaning — poured into a pattern that shapes it into a verb, a place, an instrument, or a doer. كَتَبَ (he wrote), كِتَاب (book), and مَكْتَبَة (library) all share the root ك-ت-ب ('write'). The vowels and extra letters around those three consonants belong to the pattern, not the root.

A bare root isn't itself a word you can say out loud — د-ر-س only becomes pronounceable once a pattern is applied: دَرْس (lesson), مَدْرَسَة (school, literally 'the place where studying happens'). You already know both halves of eleven such pairs — this lesson just points out the shared DNA you haven't been told about yet.

Sharing a root doesn't always predict an obvious connection in translation — جَدّ (grandfather) and جَدِيد (new) look completely unrelated in English, but they're a real, documented root family in Arabic. Recognising a root is a shortcut to guessing a new word's rough meaning, not a guarantee of the exact sense.

steps.title: Eleven root families
steps.intro: Read each pair (or trio) of words sharing a root, then the four example sentences. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Spot the shared root
steps.prompt: Which of these words shares a root with كِتَاب (book)?
steps.explanation: كِتَاب and مَكْتَبَة both come from ك-ت-ب ('write') — a book is a written thing, a library is where written things are kept.

steps.title: Numbers hiding in the weekdays
steps.prompt: الْأَحَد (Sunday) and وَاحِد (one) share a root. What does that root mean?
steps.explanation: Sunday is literally 'the first day' — five of the seven Arabic weekday names are built directly on the numbers 1–5, the same way الْخَمِيس (Thursday) is built on خَمْسَة (five).

steps.title: Not every pairing is obvious
steps.prompt: جَدّ (grandfather) and جَدِيد (new) share the same root letters ج-د-د. Are they really related?

options.label: Not obvious from the translation, but yes — a real, documented root family
No — this is just a coincidence of spelling
Yes — جَدِيد literally means "newly born person"

steps.explanation: Shared roots don't always predict an obvious sense in English — this pairing is genuine (cross-checked against Hans Wehr and Wiktionary), it just doesn't translate into a visible connection the way كِتَاب/مَكْتَبَة does.

steps.title: You've had your first look at root & pattern
steps.message: Eleven root families, all built from words you already knew — the same shared-DNA pattern behind كِتَاب/كَتَبَ/مَكْتَبَة runs through most of the Arabic vocabulary still ahead of you.
